title: The poet
hook: the poet sees and names what others feel (The Poet, 1844)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the years and the days: Emerson's line that the years teach much which the days never know. Your line was the years teach. What did looking back over one year show you? Day one thousand two hundred seven.

A friend listens to you describe a bad week, the restlessness, the checking of the phone, the way your old street keeps coming to mind. Then they say one word. "Homesick." And something clicks. That's it. The feeling didn't change, but now it has a handle, and you can pick it up and look at it. Emerson put that kind of moment, finding the word for what someone else could only carry around, near the heart of the poet's work. He wrote an essay about it called The Poet. Today, the one who names.
screen: `A BAD WEEK, DESCRIBED.` → `ONE WORD: HOMESICK.` → `NOW IT HAS A HANDLE.`

segments.voice: First, Emerson's definition. "The poet is the sayer, the namer, and represents beauty." Sayer. Namer. Not first a rhymer or a performer. The one who says what is there. Second, why we need a sayer at all. Emerson's point in the essay is that all people stand in need of expression. Everyone has the raw experience: the sunset, the loss, the love, the dread. A person can feel it all and stay quiet, not from shallowness but because the words don't come. The poet is the one in whom the words come, and when they do, the rest of us recognize our own lives. That's why a good line of poetry can feel less like news and more like being found. Third, a short phrase from the same essay: "Language is fossil poetry." Every ordinary word we use, Emerson says, was once a bright new picture someone made. Over time it hardened and got buried in everyday talk, like a shell in stone. So when you speak, you're using poems other people made, worn smooth. Fourth, what this means for anyone, poet or not. Naming is a small act of poetry. Not bad, but lonely. Not angry, but embarrassed. Not tired, but tired of being the only one who remembers. When a feeling gets its exact name, it often loosens. You can tell someone about it. You can tell yourself. Emerson's poet does this for a whole people. Anyone can do it for one afternoon.
screen: `THE SAYER, THE NAMER.` · `EVERYONE FEELS IT; THE POET SAYS IT.` · `LANGUAGE IS FOSSIL POETRY.` · `NAMING IS A SMALL POEM.` · then, large: `NAME IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one feeling precisely. Settle, and breathe. Notice what's here right now, under the surface. Give it a first word, even a rough one: fine, bad, off. Then ask, more exactly? Restless. Left out. Hopeful but scared to say so. Keep trying words, gently, the way you'd try keys in a lock, until one turns. When it does, just hold that name for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
The poet. Emerson's sayer and namer, the one who finds the words for what others feel and can't say. Today's word.
Your line: name it. Once today, when you or someone near you says fine, look for the more exact word, and say it out loud. Day one thousand two hundred seven.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson's The Poet often take it as a call to look for precise words for experience, and some keep journals or write poems for exactly that reason.

notes: Confirm exact wording: 'The poet is the sayer, the namer, and represents beauty.' and 'Language is fossil poetry.'
Confirm the paraphrase that Emerson says all people share experience and need expression, while the poet is the one able to say it.
Editor: 'the poet's whole job' softened to 'near the heart of the poet's work'; the teach now grounds its point in Emerson's own 'stand in need of expression' rather than 'the same raw experience'.
The 'homesick' hook and the naming examples are the writer's illustrations. The line that people feel and stay quiet is the writer's paraphrase of Emerson's point, softened to 'a person can'.
